analyses.title: The Iliad
analyses.author: Homer
analyses.shortDescription: Achilles' anger exposes the cost of honor, while grief opens a fragile path toward recognizing an enemy's humanity.
analyses.overview: The Iliad concentrates on a period near the end of the Trojan War, beginning with the quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon. Rather than narrating the entire war or Troy's destruction, it follows the consequences of anger, wounded status, and loss. Through an ethical lens, the epic asks whether public honor can justify suffering imposed on others. Its deepest challenge emerges when heroic achievement confronts the vulnerability shared by victors, enemies, and families.

sections.heading: When wounded honor becomes a public disaster
paragraphs: The opening dispute treats Briseis as a measure of competing male authority. Agamemnon's seizure humiliates Achilles, but both men's claims depend on a system in which a captive woman can become a transferable prize. An ethical reading therefore begins before deciding which warrior deserves sympathy. It asks whose dignity the dispute's familiar language makes easy to overlook.

Achilles' withdrawal turns a personal injury into a collective crisis. His anger has an intelligible cause: the community's leader disregards the honor on which his service depends. Yet understanding that injury does not settle whether others should pay for it. The poem dramatizes a difficult distinction between having a legitimate grievance and taking responsibility for the consequences of one's response.

sections.heading: Heroism viewed from the household
paragraphs: Hector's encounter with Andromache and their child brings the household into the heroic argument. She understands battle through the losses it threatens, while he feels the pressure of public duty and shame. Neither perspective can simply remove the other. Defending the city appears necessary, but the defense also places the family's remaining security in danger.

Their child's fear of Hector's helmet briefly interrupts the warrior's public image. The equipment that signifies honor becomes frightening when seen by someone who needs a father. This moment changes the scale of judgment. A reputation can be admired from a distance while its demands become painful within intimate life. The epic makes responsibility to a community inseparable from the vulnerable people who constitute it.

sections.heading: Grief and the escalation of revenge
paragraphs: Patroclus' death transforms Achilles' withdrawal into devastating action. His renewed fighting expresses love and grief, but these feelings do not automatically establish a just limit to retaliation. The treatment of Hector's body shows mourning becoming an attempt to deny another person the dignity of being mourned. Pain moves outward rather than finding a conclusion.

An ethical lens resists reducing this change to a lesson that anger is always wrong. Achilles' feelings matter because the narrative gives them force and intelligibility. The question is whether strong feeling authorizes unlimited action. His suffering does not cancel the suffering of Hector's family. The poem exposes how revenge can promise restored balance while multiplying the very injuries that made restoration seem necessary.

sections.heading: Recognition without an easy reconciliation
paragraphs: Priam's appeal places a bereaved father before his son's killer. By asking Achilles to remember his own father, he creates a connection that crosses the division between armies. Their encounter does not make their losses equivalent in every respect, nor does it reverse the war. It interrupts the habit of seeing an enemy only through the role that makes violence permissible.

Achilles' return of Hector's body establishes a temporary boundary within conflict. The closing emphasis on funeral rites gives attention to a life rather than celebrating a final conquest. The ethical achievement is limited but meaningful: power can acknowledge an obligation toward someone it has defeated. For contemporary readers, the epic invites judgment that includes consequences, restraint, and the dignity of those outside one's own group.

analyses.title: The Odyssey
analyses.author: Homer
analyses.shortDescription: The journey home tests more than endurance: it asks whether identity, judgment, and belonging can survive a changed world.
analyses.overview: The Odyssey follows Odysseus' difficult return to Ithaca after the Trojan War and the parallel struggles of his household. An archetypal lens traces recurring patterns of departure, trial, temptation, disguise, recognition, and return. These patterns connect the epic's varied episodes, but they do not make its hero flawless or its values universal. The homecoming becomes meaningful because survival alone cannot restore the relationships and responsibilities interrupted by absence.

sections.heading: A journey that tests the traveler
paragraphs: Odysseus repeatedly crosses boundaries between familiar human arrangements and worlds governed by unfamiliar rules. An archetypal reading sees the voyage as a sequence of thresholds that tests both ability and self-understanding. The encounters belong together because each asks whether the traveler can preserve a purpose while adapting to circumstances that defeat ordinary expectations.

The Cyclops episode complicates the resourceful-hero pattern. Cunning makes escape possible, but the desire to reveal a famous identity creates further danger. The hero's gift becomes inseparable from his weakness: intelligence can solve an immediate problem without governing pride. Reading the pattern carefully therefore means distinguishing successful action from wise action. Endurance requires learning how one's own impulses can obstruct the destination one claims to value.

sections.heading: Temptation as the loss of direction
paragraphs: Not every threat takes the form of direct violence. The Lotus-eaters make forgetting attractive, while other encounters offer pleasure, rest, or a life detached from Ithaca. In the archetype of the interrupted quest, temptation works by weakening the reason to continue. A traveler can remain physically alive while allowing the journey's purpose to disappear.

This pattern makes home a moral and imaginative orientation rather than a point on a map. Odysseus' longing gains force because other lives remain available to him. His attachment to a mortal household involves accepting limits instead of seeking an existence free from them. Yet the poem also asks whether a returning man understands what his prolonged absence has required from those whose lives he hopes to resume.

sections.heading: Those who wait also undergo trials
paragraphs: Penelope's strategies make waiting an active form of resistance. Her weaving delays the suitors while preserving space for judgment. Treating her only as the reward at the end of a male quest would erase the intelligence that helps keep a household possible. The archetype of homecoming becomes richer when the destination contains people with purposes and uncertainties of their own.

Telemachus follows a related pattern of departure and development. His search for news becomes an exercise in speaking, listening, and assuming responsibility. Father and son therefore travel through different versions of disrupted identity. One seeks restoration after long absence; the other seeks a position within an inheritance he barely knows. Their parallel journeys show that belonging develops through action rather than surviving unchanged in a person's name.

sections.heading: Recognition and the unfinished meaning of return
paragraphs: Odysseus' disguise delays recognition and makes appearance unreliable. Penelope's test involving their marriage bed turns shared knowledge into evidence that public reputation cannot provide. The reunion matters because identity is relational: someone is known through a history made with another person. Reaching Ithaca is only the physical condition for recovering that history, not a guarantee that trust will follow automatically.

The violence against the suitors and servants complicates any uncomplicated celebration of restored order. An archetypal lens identifies structures without requiring approval of every social arrangement they restore. The conclusion's need for intervention to stop further conflict also unsettles the idea that revenge produces lasting security. The epic offers perseverance and resourcefulness while asking readers to examine the power, exclusions, and human costs within a heroic return.

analyses.title: The Song of Roland
analyses.author: Anonymous
analyses.shortDescription: A remembered defeat becomes an epic of loyalty, revealing how communities turn the past into a story about belonging.
analyses.overview: The Song of Roland recounts the destruction of Charlemagne's rear guard at Roncevaux through betrayal, heroic resistance, and eventual vengeance. A historical lens separates the poem's medieval construction of the past from the earlier event it transforms. This distinction reveals how epic narrative can preserve ideals while also reorganizing memory. The work celebrates courage and feudal fidelity, but it also exposes tensions between prudent leadership, personal glory, and religiously defined collective identity.

sections.heading: Remembering an event through a later world
paragraphs: The poem reaches back to Charlemagne's Spanish campaign of 778, yet its developed account belongs to a later literary world. Einhard's Life of Charlemagne describes a mountain ambush by Gascons, commonly identified with the Basques, and names Roland among the dead. The epic transforms the encounter into a much larger conflict with a Muslim enemy and gives betrayal a central explanatory role.

The difference matters because the poem should not be used as a neutral record of the battle or of Islam. Its changes turn an unsettling military loss into a narrative with identifiable treachery, exemplary sacrifice, and eventual vindication. Historical reading examines what those transformations accomplish for an audience. Memory becomes an argument about the community's virtues rather than a transparent window onto what happened.

sections.heading: Loyalty and the danger within the community
paragraphs: Ganelon's betrayal makes internal disloyalty more threatening than open opposition. Because relationships of service and obligation sustain the poem's political world, private resentment can endanger an entire force. His actions suggest that the security of the group depends partly on promises whose enforcement cannot be reduced to military strength. A powerful army remains vulnerable when the people entrusted with its purposes pursue concealed aims.

Roland stands at the opposite pole as a figure of unwavering service, but the contrast does not eliminate disagreement over how loyalty should be practiced. Fidelity can require more than willingness to die. It can also require preserving the lives of companions. The tension prevents the ideal of loyalty from becoming entirely simple, even within a poem that strongly affirms it.

sections.heading: The horn and the cost of heroic reputation
paragraphs: Olivier urges Roland to sound the horn for help, while Roland initially treats doing so as a threat to honor. Their disagreement places two forms of courage beside each other: the refusal to appear afraid and the willingness to acknowledge danger before it becomes irreversible. The horn makes an abstract ideal concrete because its timing affects whether assistance can arrive.

Roland's eventual call preserves his determination while exposing the limits of a reputation governed by self-sufficiency. The poem honors his final struggle, so a modern reader should avoid pretending it simply rejects him. Nevertheless, Olivier's warnings allow a critical question to remain within that admiration. Can a leader's attachment to the appearance of bravery conflict with the responsibility to those whose survival depends on his judgment?

sections.heading: Faith, othering, and responsible interpretation
paragraphs: The poem divides the world through a confident religious opposition and attributes beliefs to its Muslim characters that do not accurately represent Islam. These portrayals reveal the Christian epic's imaginative construction of its adversaries. They should be analyzed as religious othering rather than repeated as factual descriptions. The language of certainty helps make violence and conversion appear part of a righteous restoration.

A historical lens makes it possible to appreciate the work's oral force, memorable conflicts, and treatment of obligation while questioning the limits of its moral community. The ending repairs order through victory and judgment, but the reader can still ask whose perspectives that order excludes. Its lasting relevance includes a warning about public storytelling: a moving account of collective identity can encourage solidarity while making the humanity of outsiders harder to perceive.

analyses.title: The Tale of Genji
analyses.author: Murasaki Shikibu
analyses.shortDescription: Behind the elegance of Heian court life, women's feelings reveal the unequal power hidden within beautiful encounters.
analyses.overview: Written by Murasaki Shikibu in early eleventh-century Japan, The Tale of Genji explores court life through intimate relationships, poetry, rank, and loss. A feminist lens examines how gender interacts with social position to shape who can pursue desire and who bears its consequences. The reading must remain sensitive to the Heian setting rather than assuming modern courtship rules. Its central argument is that aesthetic refinement does not necessarily produce equal recognition or freedom.

sections.heading: Courtly beauty and unequal room to act
paragraphs: Genji's charm, artistic gifts, and status make his attention appear valuable within the court's hierarchy. Yet those same advantages give him a freedom of movement and initiative that many women do not possess. A feminist reading asks how admiration can coexist with unequal bargaining power. The ability to inspire affection does not resolve the question of whether another person can refuse, negotiate, or leave.

Rank makes that inequality more complicated than a single division between men and women. Family connections, reputation, and access to protection shape different possibilities for different women. The novel's attention to these distinctions prevents a reading that treats every female character as interchangeable. Gender matters through concrete arrangements of dependence and prestige, rather than operating as an isolated explanation for every emotion or decision.

sections.heading: Screens, poems, and indirect forms of voice
paragraphs: Courtship often proceeds through letters, poems, intermediaries, and screens. These forms can restrict direct encounter, but they also make interpretation an important arena of agency. A reply's phrasing, timing, or refusal can communicate judgment in a setting where straightforward assertion may be difficult. Women's voices appear through such choices, even when the conditions under which they speak remain unequal.

The form of the novel reinforces that attention. Its psychological detail makes hesitation, anticipation, embarrassment, and disappointment part of the event itself. A romantic encounter cannot be understood only through the pursuit that initiates it. The reader must also consider how it is experienced by the person approached. This inward perspective complicates the attractive public image of a celebrated lover.

sections.heading: Affection and the wish to shape another person
paragraphs: Genji's relationship with the character Murasaki exposes a troubling overlap between attachment and control. His early interest in her is connected to his desire for someone resembling Fujitsubo, and his influence over her upbringing creates an unequal foundation for their later life together. A feminist interpretation asks whether being cherished can coexist with having one's identity shaped around another person's wishes.

The answer requires careful attention rather than a single label that exhausts the relationship. Murasaki's feelings and intelligence give her a life beyond the role Genji imagines. Her importance to him does not necessarily give her equal authority over their shared arrangements. The narrative's emotional force lies partly in this difference between being indispensable to someone's happiness and possessing secure freedom to determine one's own.

sections.heading: Impermanence as a pressure on privilege
paragraphs: The changing seasons and recurring awareness of loss place courtly refinement under the sign of impermanence. Beauty cannot preserve a relationship from neglect, rivalry, illness, or death. This does not make aesthetic sensitivity meaningless. It reveals its limits when appreciation remains detached from responsibility. Noticing how fleeting another person's presence is should deepen care, yet the characters do not always make that connection.

Murasaki Shikibu's authorship also matters within a world where court women produced influential Japanese writing. Their literary achievement should not be erased by treating restricted social arrangements as complete silence. Through a feminist lens, the novel offers a precise tension: women can exercise subtle cultural and interpretive authority while remaining vulnerable within intimate life. The work invites readers to examine the distance between eloquent affection and the practical conditions of respect.

learning.title: Reading across cultures and centuries
learning.body: Great Books places ancient and medieval India, the Greek epic world, Hebrew and Biblical traditions, medieval Europe, and Heian Japan in conversation without making their differences disappear. Cultural and historical context helps explain how each work imagines duty, faith, family, authority, and a meaningful life. I can compare recurring concerns while respecting the particular traditions that give them shape. Similar questions do not always produce the same answers, and a work's values should be examined through both its own circumstances and the consequences they reveal.

learning.title: Using a lens with purpose
learning.body: A literary lens is a disciplined way of directing attention. Ethical reading examines responsibility and harm; archetypal reading traces journeys and recurring patterns; feminist reading studies gender, agency, and power; historical reading distinguishes a work's setting from the circumstances of its production. No approach reveals everything. Comparing lenses helps me notice what a first interpretation overlooks. The task is to support a claim with textual details, acknowledge a lens's limits, and remain willing to revise an argument when a passage resists it.

learning.title: Moving from summary to interpretation
learning.body: Plot summary explains what happens, while analysis explains how a work creates meaning and why a detail matters. A stronger interpretation connects an event, image, contrast, or narrative choice to a clear claim. Achilles' treatment of Hector's body, Penelope's recognition test, and Roland's delayed horn call each invite arguments that go beyond recounting action. Careful analysis also distinguishes a character's belief from the work's larger perspective and separates a convincing possibility from a conclusion that the evidence cannot fully support.

learning.title: Connecting literature to responsible judgment
learning.body: Literature makes human consequences visible within decisions that might otherwise seem abstract. The course's works ask who is heard, who is protected, and who carries the cost of loyalty or ambition. As a BSCIS student, I can carry those questions into systems design, teamwork, and the treatment of information. A system's efficiency matters alongside accessibility, privacy, and its effects on people with less power. The connection is a habit of attention: identify assumptions, consider affected perspectives, and make decisions that can be explained responsibly.

reflection.question: How has your understanding and appreciation of literature changed throughout the course?
reflection.title: From finding the message to examining the question
reflection.body: I now understand literature as a way of examining difficult questions rather than a collection of plots with a single lesson at the end. The Iliad can honor courage while revealing the suffering attached to honor. The Odyssey can celebrate homecoming while leaving questions about revenge and authority unresolved. Holding these tensions together gives me a more thoughtful kind of appreciation. I do not need to agree with every value in a work to recognize how carefully it makes human conflict visible. This changes how I want to read: slowly enough to notice whose voice shapes the account and whose experience complicates it. As a fourth-year BSCIS student, I am used to looking for workable solutions. Literature reminds me that defining a problem is already an interpretive act. Before deciding what an answer should accomplish, I need to understand the people and assumptions contained in the question. That habit makes the study of old works relevant to present choices.

reflection.question: What challenges did you encounter when reading and analyzing literary masterpieces, and how did you overcome them?
reflection.title: Giving unfamiliar worlds enough time
reflection.body: The greatest challenge these works present is the distance between recognizing an action and understanding what it means within another culture. Roland's concern for reputation, the courtly exchanges in The Tale of Genji, and the obligations surrounding Greek heroism can seem obvious until I ask what assumptions support them. The language of a translation adds another difficulty because familiar English words may carry ideas that do not fully match the original setting. My response is to slow the process down: establish the sequence of events, identify the exact detail that creates uncertainty, consult reliable context, and return to the passage. I can also separate observation from interpretation in my notes so that a useful possibility does not become an unsupported fact. This method resembles debugging in one helpful respect: a precise question produces better progress than a general sense that something is confusing. The aim is not to eliminate ambiguity, but to understand which uncertainties belong to the work itself.

reflection.question: Which literary lens or approach influenced your interpretation the most, and why?
reflection.title: An ethical lens brings consequences into view
reflection.body: The ethical lens is the approach I find most influential because it asks me to look beyond a character's intention and consider who experiences the result. Achilles has reasons to feel wronged, but those reasons do not settle whether other people should suffer from his response. Roland's courage is compelling, yet his refusal to call for help raises questions about responsibility toward his companions. These examples make interpretation more demanding than choosing a hero and defending every action he takes. I can recognize courage, grief, or loyalty while still examining the limits of what they justify. The lens also encourages me to consider people outside the central conflict, including captives, families, and those who cannot control the decision. For BSCIS, this perspective has practical value. A technically successful system can still place an unfair burden on its users. Asking who benefits, who bears risk, and who has a meaningful choice helps me connect literary judgment with the responsibilities of designing and using technology.

reflection.question: What important realizations about life, society, culture, or human nature have you gained?
reflection.title: Admiration needs room for a second perspective
reflection.body: A realization I take from these works is that admiration becomes more responsible when it allows another perspective to interrupt it. Genji's refinement does not remove the unequal conditions of his relationships. The Song of Roland creates solidarity through a powerful account of collective identity, but its religious divisions also show how a community can misrepresent outsiders. The Iliad makes a similar interruption possible when Priam's grief reaches Achilles across the boundary between enemies. These are different literary worlds, so I should not flatten them into one universal message. Together, however, they encourage a habit of looking for the person hidden by a confident label. A hero, an enemy, a leader, or a user remains a person situated within relationships and constraints. This matters in social life because a convenient description can make judgment feel complete before understanding has begun. I want to keep the ability to evaluate actions clearly while resisting the assumption that a single role explains an entire human being.

reflection.question: How can you apply the lessons and values learned from Great Books in your personal, academic, or future professional life?
reflection.title: Carrying attentive judgment into technology and everyday life
reflection.body: I can apply Great Books by making careful interpretation part of ordinary decisions. In academic work, that means distinguishing evidence from assumption, acknowledging sources, and revising an argument when a stronger explanation appears. In personal relationships, it means listening long enough to understand why another person describes the same situation differently. In a future BSCIS role, I want these habits to influence how I understand requirements and evaluate systems. Before calling a process efficient, I can ask whether people can use it, whether their information is protected, and whether its failures fall most heavily on those with the least control. Penelope's careful recognition, Olivier's attention to consequences, and Priam's appeal to shared vulnerability offer different reminders to pause before accepting an easy account. The realistic application is not to treat a literary character as a technical rule. It is to practice asking better questions, explain decisions honestly, and remain accountable to the people affected by what I help build.
